title: Forge: your evidence-based programme
tagline: A one-year, five-phase plan for an athletic, lean physique, with the science behind every decision.
welcome:
This app is your complete training, nutrition and recovery programme, built from your intake profile and from the research evidence, with every significant decision explained.

**How to start**

1. Read the [[plan:safety|safety and stop rules]] (five minutes).
2. Skim the [[page:programme|programme overview]] and your [[page:profile|profile analysis]].
3. Set up your logging app ([[plan:logging|how]]).
4. Press **Start Phase 0 · week 1** below. Phase 0 is a light orientation week: you learn the machines, record a baseline, and keep eating as usual while you weigh in daily and log your food (continue this through Phase 1 weeks 1–2 to calibrate your maintenance intake).

Each session has a warm-up, main training and a cool-down with stretching. Open a session to read or copy it, or press **Start guided session** in the gym for step-by-step timers.
disclaimer: This programme is for personal use by a healthy adult. It is built from published evidence and documented reasoning, not from a medical examination, and it is not medical advice. Stop and seek care if any warning sign in the [[plan:safety|safety rules]] occurs. Evidence was searched up to 28 October 2026 (30 October 2026 for training without equipment); summaries are written in our own words from abstracts or full texts, and every source is listed with its DOI or PMID so you can check it.

sections.title: 1 · Your data
sections.body:
Everything below is computed from your self-reported intake profile. Measurements were self-taken and the method and time of day were not recorded, so treat each as approximate (as a rule of thumb, tape measurements vary by about 1 cm between attempts; Phase 0 re-measures everything under a standard protocol).

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Age, sex | 31, male |
| Height, weight | 181 cm, 77 kg (stable for 6 months) |
| Circumferences (cm) | neck 38 · shoulders 118 · chest 96 · waist at navel 86 · narrowest waist 81 · hip 96 · arm flexed 33 / relaxed 30 · thigh upper 62 / mid 51 · wrist 17 · elbow 27 · knee 37 · ankle 23 |
| Shoulder breadth | 40 cm |
| Training history | none; no sport; no coaching |
| Baseline tests | 5 push-ups · 3 pull-ups · 60 s plank |
| Movement screens | deep squat with heels down and neutral back ✔ · overhead reach without lumbar arching ✔ · half-kneeling lunge upright ✔ · cannot reach toes with straight knees ✘ |
| Single-leg stance | right 30 s eyes open / 15 s eyes closed · left 20 s / 10 s |
| Schedule | wake 12:00 · train ~13:00 · work 16:00–01:00 (desk) · sleep ~04:00–12:00 (7–8 h, 'OK but not great') |
| Activity | 5,000–8,000 steps/day |
| Diet | omnivore, cooks own meals, 4 meals/day, willing to track, ₹20,000/month |
| Supplements | creatine, magnesium glycinate, B12, folic acid, D3, K2, omega-3, caffeine (~100 mg/day), L-theanine (doses unknown) |
| Health | no conditions, injuries, medications, exertional symptoms or family history of early heart disease; no alcohol or smoking |

sections.title: 2 · Body composition estimates
sections.body:
No method you have can measure body fat directly; each estimates it with an error of several percentage points. Three independent equations were applied to your numbers:

| Method | Inputs | Your result | Typical error | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US Navy circumference equation | neck, navel waist, height | **16.7%** | 4–6 points | Underestimated DXA body fat by about 4–6 points on average in men in a large military sample [@McClung2025_CBEvsDXA; @Friedl1997_circumferenceDXA] |
| Relative fat mass (RFM) | height, navel waist | **21.9%** (19.3% with the narrowest waist) | ≈3–4 points (inference; not reported in the sources) | Developed against DXA; no systematic bias in a small validation [@Woolcott2018_RFM; @GuzmanLeon2019_RFMvalidation] |
| Deurenberg BMI equation | BMI, age, sex | **19.1%** | SEE 4.1 points | Cannot distinguish muscle from fat, so it will become increasingly misleading as you gain muscle [@Deurenberg1991_BMIequation] |

**Working estimate: about 20% body fat (plausible range ≈17–24%).** The Navy value is shifted up to account for its known bias, and RFM's navel value sits in the same range. This places you in the normal-to-moderate range for a man of your age: lean enough that building muscle while losing fat (recomposition) is realistic.

**Fat-free mass (FFM)** at 20% body fat ≈ 61.6 kg (range ≈58.5–63.9 kg). **Fat-free mass index (FFMI)** = FFM / height² ≈ **18.8 kg/m²** (range ≈17.9–19.5), close to the median for young men (≈18.9) [@Schutz2002_FFMIpercentiles]. Drug-free athletes in a classic study rarely exceeded a normalised FFMI of about 25 [@Kouri1995_FFMI], so you have substantial room to add muscle before approaching any natural ceiling.

**Your scale's body-fat reading** will add a fourth number, but consumer foot-to-foot impedance scales disagree with reference methods (DXA or multi-compartment models) by roughly ±5–6 percentage points for an individual reading, even though they repeat themselves closely [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices; @Nana2022_footBIAvsDXA; @Nickerson2019_FFBIAmen]. See [[plan:monitoring]] for how (and how not) to use it.

sections.title: 3 · Energy expenditure
sections.body:
| Estimate | Method | kcal/day |
|---|---|---|
| Resting energy (REE) | Mifflin–St Jeor (weight, height, age, sex) | 1,751 |
| Resting energy | Katch–McArdle / Cunningham (from FFM 58.5–63.9 kg) | ≈1,630–1,910 |
| Total expenditure, before training | REE × PAL 1.4–1.5 (desk job, 5,000–8,000 steps) | ≈2,450–2,630 |
| Total expenditure, training 3–4×/week + more steps | REE × PAL 1.6–1.7 | ≈2,800–2,980 |
| Reference values | US National Academies equations, 'inactive' to 'low active' | ≈2,680–2,900 |

Mifflin–St Jeor is the best-supported general equation, most often within 10% of measured resting expenditure, but clinically important errors still occur for individuals [@Mifflin1990_REE; @Frankenfield2005_RMRequationsSR]. In one Singapore study, Asian Indian men had lower measured resting expenditure than Chinese men of the same size (by roughly 50–70 kcal/day), so the true value could be somewhat lower than predicted [@Song2016_AsianIndianREE]. **Provisional maintenance: ≈2,700 kcal/day (plausible 2,450–2,900).**

Your weight has been stable for six months, so your current intake already roughly equals your current expenditure. In Phase 0 and the first two weeks of Phase 1 you weigh in daily and log your food (a reliable trend needs 2–3 weeks); if your weight stays flat, your logged intake becomes your calibrated maintenance, which beats any equation. Food logs tend to under-report intake (by almost half in one small study of adults with obesity; probably much less in careful trackers who weigh food, an inference) [@Lichtman1992_underreporting], so the weight trend has the final say ([[rule:energy-adjustment]]).

sections.title: 4 · Fitness and movement baseline
sections.body:
- **Muscular endurance:** 5 push-ups and 3 pull-ups indicate low upper-body strength-endurance relative to body weight, which is expected for someone who has never trained and improves quickly. Push-up capacity was associated with lower cardiovascular risk in an observational cohort of firefighters (association, not proof of cause) [@Yang2019_pushups].
- **Balance:** under a standard protocol, men aged 18–39 average about 44 s eyes open and about 17 s eyes closed (best of three; very wide spread) [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]. Your eyes-open times (30 s right, 20 s left) are below that, and your left leg is about one-third worse than your right. Leg dominance does not explain such a gap at group level [@Schorderet2021_dominance]. Balance improves fast with practice but mainly on the practised task [@Kummel2016_specificity].
- **Flexibility:** not reaching your toes with straight knees reflects limited extensibility of the whole posterior chain (hamstrings, hips, spine, possibly neural tissue), not the hamstrings alone [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test]. Your squat, overhead-reach and half-kneeling screens are good, so there is no obvious restriction elsewhere.
- **Aerobic fitness:** unknown; Phase 0 estimates it with a walking test [@Kline1987_Rockport]. Age-predicted maximum heart rate ≈186 bpm (Tanaka equation), but an individual's true value can differ by about ±20 bpm [@Tanaka2001_HRmax; @Nes2013_HUNT_HRmax], which is why effort and the talk test, not heart-rate zones, guide your aerobic training.

sections.title: 5 · Health markers
sections.body:
| Marker | Your value | Reference | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Waist-to-height ratio | 0.48 (navel) · 0.45 (narrowest) | < 0.5 healthy boundary [@Ashwell2012_WHtR; @NICE2025_NG246] | Below the boundary |
| Waist circumference | 86 cm (navel) · 81 cm (narrowest) | Consensus action threshold for Asian Indian men ≥90 cm [@Misra2009_AsianIndianConsensus]; one Indian study found ≈78 cm best identified men with at least one cardiovascular risk factor (sensitivity 74%, specificity 68%) [@Misra2006_IndianWaist] | Below the consensus threshold but above the lower data-driven cut-off; one more reason to bring the waist down during recomposition |
| BMI | 23.5 kg/m² | WHO suggested 23 as an action point for Asian populations [@WHO2004_AsianBMI] | Slightly above that point, but BMI cannot separate muscle from fat; waist-based markers are more informative for you and BMI will rise as you gain muscle |

The waist is the most useful number to track: its link with health does not depend much on the exact site measured [@Ross2008_waistprotocol], but values differ by site, so always use the same one (the navel is used for decisions here).

sections.title: 6 · Ambiguities, gaps and how they were resolved
sections.body:
Nothing in your profile required a question before starting: each gap is handled by an assumption stated here or by a rule that adapts to your own data.

| Ambiguity or gap | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Measurements self-taken, method unknown | Re-measured in Phase 0 under a standard protocol; baseline numbers above treated as approximate |
| Two waist values (81 and 86 cm) | Navel used for the Navy equation and for decisions; the narrowest waist is tracked as a second marker |
| Body fat unknown; the three equations disagree | Working estimate 20% (17–24%); decisions use waist and weight trends, not a body-fat number |
| Food intake and protein intake unknown | Calibration through Phase 0 and Phase 1 weeks 1–2 (logging plus daily weigh-ins); provisional targets until then |
| Supplement doses unknown | The [[plan:supplements|supplement review]] gives evidence-based doses and upper limits for you to compare with your labels |
| Location not stated (₹ budget suggests India) | Assumed India for foods, climate (heat), supplement regulation and vitamin D/B12 context; nothing else depends on it |
| Work days per week and commute unknown | Sessions fit 13:00–14:10 so you can eat and prepare before 16:00; each session has a short version; the week can shift if your days off differ |
| Resting heart rate and VO₂max unknown | Measured in Phase 0 (manual pulse; walking test) |
| Dominant leg unknown | Not needed: the left leg is treated as the weaker side because of your balance results |
| Training 1 h after waking | Longer warm-ups; consistent training time; the body adapts to a habitual training time [@Grgic2019_timeOfDayTraining] |
| Wearable undecided | Nothing requires one; see [[dec:D25]] |
| Separate mobility sessions 'not now, possibly later' | Mobility and stretching are built into every warm-up and cool-down; an optional 5-minute daily routine is offered in [[plan:activity]] |

sections.title: 7 · Where your goals compete, and how they are arbitrated
sections.body:
- **Muscle gain vs fat loss.** Building muscle is easiest with a small energy surplus; losing fat requires a deficit. Because you are untrained and not very lean, you can do both at once (recomposition) at a small deficit, so Phase 1 eats at maintenance to about 300 kcal below it; later phases choose between a small surplus and maintenance using your waist and strength trends ([[dec:D04]], [[rule:phase-nutrition]]).
- **'High muscle mass' vs 'not bulky'.** Muscle accrues slowly (on average about 1.5 kg of lean mass per ~10 weeks early on [@Benito2020_wholeBodyHypertrophy], then less each year, an inference), so bulkiness is not a near-term risk, and the [[rule:size-control|size-control rule]] lets you stop any muscle growing once it looks right.
- **Muscle vs flexibility.** Full-range resistance training improves range of motion about as much as stretching [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROMmeta]; muscle gained this way does not make you stiff.
- **Hypertrophy vs VO₂max and endurance.** At the aerobic doses used here, on separate days, cardio does not measurably reduce muscle or strength gains in untrained people [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA]; aerobic work therefore grows across the year rather than being postponed.
- **Many lower-priority goals (agility, coordination, balance, mobility).** These are trained efficiently inside warm-ups and through a skill you enjoy rather than with separate sessions, consistent with your preference ([[dec:D17]]).

Feasibility and timelines are discussed in [[sci:sci-expectations]] and [[dec:D26]].
